## Introduction

I wanted to explore how New Jersey's housing market changed over the past decade. My question is: **How did New Jersey's house-price index change between 2016 and 2026, and which years showed the largest year-over-year increases?** This vignette demonstrates `readr`, `dplyr`, `tidyr`, and `ggplot2` using real government housing data.

**Data:** A fixed snapshot (retrieved November 15, 2026; FRED last updated August 25, 2026) of the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) *All-Transactions House Price Index for New Jersey*, available through the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED), series `NJSTHPI`. It measures changes in house prices using sales and appraisal data and is **not a median sale price or a dollar amount**. The series is quarterly, not seasonally adjusted, and indexed to 1980 Q1 = 100. See [the FRED series and metadata](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NJSTHPI) and [FHFA's methodology and data](https://www.fhfa.gov/data/house-price-index).

**Important limitation:** As of November 15, 2026, the confirmed observations extend through **2026 Q2**. To compare years fairly, our annual comparison uses the **second quarter of every year**, not incomplete annual averages. FRED may revise its live series later, but the snapshot here remains unchanged for reproducibility.

## 1. Import an official, fixed data snapshot

I used a **fixed snapshot** of the official FHFA series copied from the [FRED NJSTHPI data table](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/NJSTHPI), last updated August 25, 2026. Embedding these published values means every classmate can render the assignment offline, without an API key or external CSV. The `readr::read_csv()` function still demonstrates importing CSV-formatted data; here the CSV is embedded directly in the document.

```{r}
# Install tidyverse once in the R console if needed:
# install.packages("tidyverse")

nj_raw <- readr::read_csv(I(nj_csv), show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## 2. Clean and filter the data

```{r}
nj_housing <- nj_raw %>%
  transmute(
    date = as.Date(date),
    price_index = as.numeric(NJSTHPI),
    year = as.integer(format(date, "%Y")),
    month = as.integer(format(date, "%m")),
    quarter = paste0("Q", (month - 1) %/% 3 + 1)
  ) %>%
  filter(year >= 2016, year <= 2026, !is.na(price_index)) %>%
  arrange(date)

# Check that there are observations for the requested period.
stopifnot(nrow(nj_housing) > 0, any(nj_housing$year == 2016),
          any(nj_housing$year == 2026))

nj_housing %>% select(date, year, quarter, price_index) %>% tail(8)
```

`transmute()` creates a smaller, analysis-ready table; `filter()` keeps 2016–2026 observations; and `arrange()` sorts them. I also used simple date operations to label each quarter. `stopifnot()` provides an early warning if the source does not contain the years needed.

## 3. Inspect how complete each year is

```{r}
quarter_coverage <- nj_housing %>%
  count(year, name = "quarters_available") %>%
  mutate(complete_year = quarters_available == 4)

quarter_coverage
```

`count()` tallies quarterly observations by year, and `mutate()` labels whether each year has all four quarters. This prevents us from treating 2026 as a completed year.

## 4. Compare the same quarter each year

I choose Q2 because it is available in both the starting year (2016) and the latest confirmed year (2026). Comparing the same quarter helps reduce the influence of normal seasonal patterns, although the index itself is not seasonally adjusted.

```{r}
nj_q2 <- nj_housing %>%
  filter(quarter == "Q2") %>%
  arrange(year) %>%
  mutate(
    previous_year_index = lag(price_index),
    yoy_change_pct = 100 * (price_index / previous_year_index - 1),
    index_2016_q2_100 = 100 * price_index / first(price_index)
  )

nj_q2 %>%
  select(year, price_index, yoy_change_pct, index_2016_q2_100) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))
```

`lag()` looks back one row, so after sorting it lets us compare a quarter against the same quarter one year earlier. `mutate()` calculates the **year-over-year percentage change** and also expresses the index relative to 2016 Q2 = 100. The 2016 year-over-year change is missing because 2015 was intentionally excluded.

The relative index shows transformation: if it equals 150, that corresponds to a 50% increase in the source index since 2016 Q2, **not** a home price of $150 or a 50% increase in every individual property's value.

## 5. Finding the biggest and smallest annual changes

```{r}
changes_ranked <- nj_q2 %>%
  filter(!is.na(yoy_change_pct)) %>%
  arrange(desc(yoy_change_pct)) %>%
  select(year, yoy_change_pct)

changes_ranked %>%
  mutate(yoy_change_pct = round(yoy_change_pct, 2))

# The two extremes, identified from the data rather than hard-coded.
changes_ranked %>%
  slice(c(1, n()))
```

`arrange(desc(...))` sorts from largest to smallest percentage change. `slice()` selects specific rows. This makes it easy to identify years worth investigating, without assuming that price changes were the same everywhere in New Jersey.

## 6. Pivot the quarterly data into a comparison table

```{r}
recent_quarters <- nj_housing %>%
  filter(year >= 2024) %>%
  select(year, quarter, price_index) %>%
  mutate(quarter = factor(quarter, levels = paste0("Q", 1:4))) %>%
  complete(year, quarter) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = quarter, values_from = price_index) %>%
  arrange(year)

recent_quarters
```

`complete()` makes absent year-quarter combinations explicit, and `pivot_wider()` turns quarter labels into columns. Missing values for quarters not yet published appear as `NA`—they are **not zeroes**.

## 7. Visualizing all quarterly observations

```{r}
ggplot(nj_housing, aes(x = date, y = price_index)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "#1F648A") +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, color = "#1F648A") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "New Jersey House-Price Index, 2016–2026",
    subtitle = "Quarterly FHFA all-transactions index; 2026 is partial",
    x = "Quarter", y = "House-price index (1980 Q1 = 100)",
    caption = "Source: FHFA via FRED, series NJSTHPI; not seasonally adjusted"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

`ggplot()` maps the date and index to axes, `geom_line()` reveals the long-term trend, and `geom_point()` makes the actual quarterly observations visible. This plot shows index levels, **not** dollar-denominated home prices.

## 8. Visualize year-over-year growth

```{r}
nj_q2 %>%
  filter(!is.na(yoy_change_pct)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = yoy_change_pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#287E75") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "New Jersey Year-over-Year House-Price Index Change",
    subtitle = "Q2 versus Q2 of the previous year, 2017–2026",
    x = "Year", y = "Change from previous Q2 (%)",
    caption = "Source: FHFA via FRED, NJSTHPI; 2026 includes Q2 data"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

`geom_col()` displays already-calculated numbers. Here each bar is the percent change between two Q2 observations. A taller positive bar signals faster index growth, rather than necessarily higher affordability costs for a specific buyer.

## 9. Summarize the decade in one calculation

```{r}
start_index <- nj_q2 %>% filter(year == 2016) %>% pull(price_index)
end_index <- nj_q2 %>% filter(year == 2026) %>% pull(price_index)

decade_change_pct <- 100 * (end_index / start_index - 1)

tibble(
  period = "2016 Q2 to 2026 Q2",
  starting_index = start_index,
  ending_index = end_index,
  cumulative_change_pct = round(decade_change_pct, 2)
)
```

`pull()` extracts a column as a vector, allowing us to calculate the cumulative percentage change between two comparable points in time. A decade-long percentage change is **not** the same as an annual growth rate.

## Conclusion

This vignette shows how the TidyVerse helps turn an official housing time series into a clear, reproducible analysis. `readr` imports data, `dplyr` cleans and compares observations, `tidyr` reshapes the data, and `ggplot2` creates visual explanations. The key methodological choice is to compare Q2 across years, since 2026 does not yet have all four quarters in the confirmed source data. The result describes statewide house-price **index movements**, not local home-sale prices, rent costs, mortgage payments, or whether buying is more affordable for a particular family.

## Reproducibility and references

- **Data source:** U.S. Federal Housing Finance Agency, *All-Transactions House Price Index for New Jersey* (`NJSTHPI`), retrieved through [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NJSTHPI).
- **Verified source table for the embedded CSV:** `https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/NJSTHPI` (42 quarterly observations, 2016 Q1–2026 Q2).
- **Requirements:** R, the `tidyverse` package, and Quarto. No internet connection, credentials, local file paths, or additional submitted data files are needed when rendering.
- **Data freshness:** This is a fixed snapshot of FRED observations last updated August 25, 2026, not a live feed. Future source revisions will not automatically alter this vignette. The comparison is anchored to Q2 observations for 2016–2026.
